Can you draft the paragraph and include 2–3 credible academic sources I can cite?","plus_response":"Absolutely—here’s a draft you can use (300–400 words) plus a citation-ready source list.

Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT) both explain motivation by identifying distinct mechanisms through which learners decide to engage and persist, yet they foreground different drivers of effort. SDT emphasizes the quality of motivation as rooted in basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness; when these needs are supported, individuals internalize goals and shift from controlled forms of motivation toward more self-endorsed regulation, which is associated with greater persistence and conceptual learning. In contrast, EVT frames motivation as a function of expectancy (beliefs about success) and subjective task values—most commonly intrinsic interest, utility value, attainment value, and perceived cost—so effort and persistence follow from learners’ evaluations of both capability and the worth of the task. Empirically, SDT research often operationalizes need satisfaction through perceptions of choice, feedback, and belonging, linking these experiences to sustained engagement even when external incentives are weak. EVT studies, meanwhile, frequently manipulate or measure task beliefs and value appraisals, showing that increasing expected success and clarifying the relevance of tasks can raise performance and persistence, particularly for learners facing uncertainty or low utility.

Taken together, SDT and EVT offer complementary perspectives: SDT explains how motivational processes become internalized through supportive social contexts, whereas EVT specifies how specific beliefs and value components translate into engagement decisions. A synthesis suggests that autonomy-supportive instruction may improve expectancies and perceived values, thereby strengthening the motivational pathways that govern effort. To support a coherent argument in a class paper, you can discuss SDT as a framework for how contexts shape internal regulation, and EVT as a framework for how learners’ expectancy and value judgments determine the magnitude of effort.

Sources to cite (credible, academic):
1) Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (2000). The “what” and “why” of goal pursuits: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior. *Psychological Inquiry, 11*(4), 227–268.
2) Eccles, J. S., & Wigfield, A. (2002). Motivational beliefs, values, and goals. *Annual Review of Psychology, 53*, 109–132.
3) Wigfield, A., & Eccles, J. S. (2000). Expectancy–value theory of achievement motivation. *Contemporary Educational Psychology, 25*(1), 68–81.","minus_response":"Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT) both explain motivation and persistence, but they do so via different constructs. SDT argues that motivation quality depends on how well three basic needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—are supported; when learners feel choice, effective mastery, and social connection, they internalize goals and show more sustained, self-endorsed engagement rather than merely complying due to external pressure. EVT, in contrast, models motivation as a product of expectancy (beliefs about one’s likelihood of success) and task value. Task value includes intrinsic interest, utility, attainment value, and perceived cost, implying that learners will invest effort when they expect they can succeed and when the task seems worth doing. As a result, SDT is often operationalized through perceptions of need support (e.g., autonomy-supportive instruction and feedback), whereas EVT is operationalized through belief and value assessments (e.g., students’ perceived competence and the usefulness or importance of the work).

Comparing the theories highlights complementarity: SDT provides a rationale for why motivational processes become internalized through supportive learning environments, while EVT specifies how expectancy and value appraisals drive the level of effort and persistence in the moment. In a synthesis, autonomy-supportive contexts may strengthen expectancy and increase perceived value by improving feelings of competence and relevance, thereby amplifying engagement.
